\begin{codebox}{Box 3}{The stochastic block model, with graph-tool}
import graph_tool.all as gt
gt.seed_rng(1)
g = gt.Graph(directed=False)
g.add_edge_list(karate.get_edgelist())
state = gt.minimize_blockmodel_dl(g, state_args=dict(deg_corr=False))
sbm = state.get_blocks().a
print(sbm)
\end{codebox}
\begin{linenotes}
\item[1] graph-tool is a second library. It fits the stochastic block model, which you know from the lecture. \texttt{as gt} is its short name.
\item[2] The fit makes random choices. \texttt{seed\_rng(1)} fixes them, so that everyone in the room gets the same answer. Change the \texttt{1} and you may get a different grouping.
\item[3] graph-tool cannot read igraph's networks. It has its own kind, so we start with an empty one. \texttt{directed=False} says that a friendship goes both ways.
\item[4] \texttt{karate.get\_edgelist()} asks igraph for all the friendships as pairs of node numbers. \texttt{add\_edge\_\allowbreak list} hands the pairs to graph-tool, which creates the nodes and the edges. This line is the only bridge between the two libraries.
\item[5] \texttt{minimize\_blockmodel\_dl} fits the stochastic block model. \texttt{dl} stands for \emph{description length}: of all the ways to group the nodes, it picks the one that describes the network in the fewest bits. It decides the number of groups too. \texttt{state\_args=dict(deg\_corr=False)} asks for the plain model of the lecture, where the group alone decides how likely a friendship is. Graph-tool's default lets every member also have a number of friends of their own; on a network this small, that version finds one single group, which tells us nothing. The fitted model is stored as \texttt{state}.
\item[6] \texttt{state.get\_blocks()} gives the group of each node, in graph-tool's own array type. \texttt{.a} turns it into a plain array of numbers, like the list in Box 2.
\item[7] Print it: again one number for each of the 34 nodes.
\end{linenotes}
